concepts.name: Origins and Historical Context of the Three Buddhist Schools
key_dimensions: Chronological emergence: Theravada (oldest) → Mahayana (1st century BCE/CE) → Vajrayana (7th century CE)
Role of Buddhist Councils in crystallizing sectarian differences, especially the 4th Council under Kanishka
Geographic spread: Theravada to Southeast Asia, Mahayana to East Asia, Vajrayana to Tibet/Nepal
UPSC trap: Distinguishing which council caused the Theravada-Mahayana split (2nd Council at Vaishali vs. 4th Council at Kundalavana)

concepts.name: The Bodhisattva Ideal vs. Arahant Ideal: Core Philosophical Divergence
key_dimensions: Arahant ideal in Theravada: individual liberation (Nibbana) as the highest goal
Bodhisattva ideal in Mahayana: postponing personal liberation to help all sentient beings attain enlightenment
Implication for religious practice: Mahayana's emphasis on compassion (Karuna) and skillful means (Upaya)
UPSC trap: Conflating Bodhisattva with Buddha — Bodhisattvas are beings on the path, not yet fully enlightened

concepts.name: Concept of Sunyata (Emptiness) in Mahayana Philosophy
key_dimensions: Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka school: all phenomena are empty of inherent existence (Sunyata)
Contrast with Theravada Abhidhamma: which accepts ultimate realities (dharmas) as truly existent
Yogacara school (Asanga/Vasubandhu): 'Mind-only' (Vijnanavada) as an alternative Mahayana metaphysics
UPSC trap: Sunyata is NOT nihilism — it is the middle path between eternalism and annihilationism

concepts.name: Theravada Canon: The Pali Tipitaka
key_dimensions: Three 'baskets': Vinaya Pitaka (monastic rules), Sutta Pitaka (discourses), Abhidhamma Pitaka (philosophical analysis)
Language: Pali — significance as the language closest to Magadhi Prakrit spoken by the Buddha
Key texts: Dhammapada, Milindapanha, Visuddhimagga (Buddhaghosa's commentary)
UPSC trap: Tipitaka was NOT written during Buddha's lifetime; first compiled at the 1st Buddhist Council (Rajagriha)

concepts.name: Mahayana Sutras and Their Philosophical Significance
key_dimensions: Key texts: Prajnaparamita Sutras (Heart Sutra, Diamond Sutra), Lotus Sutra (Saddharmapundarika), Vimalakirti Sutra
Concept of 'eternal Buddha' in Lotus Sutra vs. historical Buddha in Theravada
Trikaya doctrine (Three Bodies of Buddha): Dharmakaya, Sambhogakaya, Nirmanakaya — unique to Mahayana
UPSC trap: Mahayana sutras are NOT accepted as authentic by Theravada; regarded as later compositions

concepts.name: Vajrayana: Tantric Buddhism — Origins, Practices, and Texts
key_dimensions: Emerged in Bengal/Bihar (Pala period, 7th–12th century CE); influenced by Shaiva Tantra
Key concepts: Mantra, Mandala, Mudra, and the role of the Guru (Vajracharya/Lama)
Tantric texts: Guhyasamaja Tantra, Hevajra Tantra; use of esoteric rituals for swift liberation
UPSC trap: Vajrayana is NOT a separate religion; it is a 'vehicle' (yana) within Mahayana, not outside it

concepts.name: The Three Yanas: Hinayana, Mahayana, and Vajrayana — Classification and Controversy
key_dimensions: 'Hinayana' (Lesser Vehicle) as a pejorative Mahayana label — modern scholars prefer 'Theravada' or 'Nikaya Buddhism'
Yana (vehicle) as a soteriological path — Shravakayana, Pratyekabuddhayana, Bodhisattvayana
Vajrayana as 'Mantrayana' or 'Tantrayana' — claims to be the fastest path to Buddhahood
UPSC trap: 'Hinayana' ≠ Theravada exclusively; refers to 18 early schools, only one of which (Sthaviravada) survives as Theravada

concepts.name: Role of Nalanda and Vikramashila Universities in Mahayana and Vajrayana Transmission
key_dimensions: Nalanda (Bihar): center of Mahayana learning; patronized by Guptas, Harshavardhana, Palas
Vikramashila (Bihar): established by Pala king Dharmapala specifically for Vajrayana studies
Key scholars: Nagarjuna, Asanga, Vasubandhu, Dharmakirti, Atisha (Dipankara) at these institutions
UPSC trap: Nalanda was destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khilji (1193 CE) — NOT during the Gupta period

concepts.name: Buddhist Councils: Role in Sectarian Developments
key_dimensions: 1st Council (Rajagriha, 483 BCE): compilation of Vinaya and Dharma after Buddha's Mahaparinirvana
2nd Council (Vaishali, 383 BCE): dispute over Vinaya rules → first major schism (Sthaviravada vs. Mahasanghika)
3rd Council (Pataliputra, 250 BCE): under Ashoka; expulsion of heretics; dispatch of missions
4th Council (Kashmir, 1st century CE, under Kanishka): consolidation of Sarvastivada/Mahayana; Theravada DID NOT participate

concepts.name: The Concept of Nirvana/Nibbana: Theravada vs. Mahayana Interpretations
key_dimensions: Theravada: Nibbana as cessation of craving (Tanha), escape from Samsara — transcendent but not a 'place'
Mahayana: distinguishes between 'Hinayana Nirvana' (mere cessation) and 'Parinirvana' (full Buddhahood with Sunyata realization)
Vajrayana: Nirvana and Samsara are non-dual (advaita-like position) — liberation within the world
UPSC trap: Buddha described Nirvana negatively (what it is NOT) — it is NOT annihilation (Uccheda) nor eternal existence (Sassata)

concepts.name: Spread of Buddhism to Southeast and East Asia: Role of Different Schools
key_dimensions: Theravada transmission: Sri Lanka (Mahinda/Sanghamitta) → Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, Laos
Mahayana transmission: Central Asia → China (Han dynasty onward), Korea, Japan, Vietnam
Vajrayana transmission: India → Tibet (7th century CE, Padmasambhava), Bhutan, Mongolia
UPSC trap: Japan has BOTH Mahayana (Zen, Pure Land) AND Vajrayana (Shingon) traditions — not exclusively one school

concepts.name: Stupa Architecture and Iconography: Evolution Across Buddhist Schools
key_dimensions: Theravada stupas: reliquary mounds (Sanchi, Amaravati) — aniconic representation of Buddha (footprints, wheel, Bodhi tree)
Shift to anthropomorphic Buddha images: Gandhara (Greco-Roman influence) and Mathura schools — associated with Mahayana rise
Vajrayana iconography: mandalas, wrathful deities (Mahakala), Yab-Yum imagery representing union of wisdom and compassion
UPSC trap: The iconic Buddha image did NOT originate with Theravada; aniconic art preceded iconic representations in ALL early schools

concepts.name: Ashoka's Role in Buddhist Propagation and Its Sectarian Implications
key_dimensions: Ashoka's personal affiliation: primarily associated with Theravada (Sthaviravada) tradition
Missions sent after 3rd Council: Mahinda to Sri Lanka, missionaries to Greek kingdoms, Southeast Asia
Ashoka's Dhamma vs. sectarian Buddhism: his edicts emphasize moral conduct, NOT specific Buddhist doctrine
UPSC trap: Ashoka's edicts do NOT use the term 'Buddhism'; they reference 'Dhamma' which had broader, non-sectarian meaning

concepts.name: Mahayana's Pantheon of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas
key_dimensions: Key Bodhisattvas: Avalokiteshvara (compassion), Manjushri (wisdom), Vajrapani (power), Ksitigarbha (guardian of hell realms)
Celestial Buddhas: Amitabha (Pure Land), Akshobhya, Vairochana — concept of multiple simultaneous Buddhas
Pure Land Buddhism (Sukhavati): devotional path to Amitabha's paradise — reflects Bhakti-like development in Mahayana
UPSC trap: Avalokiteshvara becomes Guanyin (female) in China — same Bodhisattva, gender transformation in cultural transmission

concepts.name: Decline of Buddhism in India: Multifactorial Analysis
key_dimensions: Internal factors: monasticism divorced from lay society, Vajrayana's esoteric practices limiting mass appeal, corruption in monasteries
External factors: Islamic invasions destroying Nalanda/Vikramashila, Brahmanical revival (Shankaracharya's Advaita absorbing Buddhist ideas)
Absorption thesis: Buddha incorporated as 9th avatar of Vishnu in Puranic Hinduism — undermining Buddhist distinctiveness
UPSC trap: Buddhism did NOT decline uniformly — it persisted in Bengal under Palas until 12th century CE; Theravada never strongly rooted in north India

concepts.name: Pratityasamutpada (Dependent Origination): Universal Buddhist Doctrine and School-wise Interpretations
key_dimensions: Core teaching across ALL schools: all phenomena arise dependently; nothing exists independently — the 12 Nidanas (chain of causation)
Theravada interpretation: causal sequence explaining rebirth and suffering in psychological terms
Mahayana (Madhyamaka): Dependent origination = Sunyata — things have no inherent existence because they arise dependently
UPSC trap: Pratityasamutpada is the philosophical foundation of BOTH the doctrine of Anatta (no-self) AND Anicca (impermanence)

concepts.name: Pala Dynasty: Patronage of Vajrayana and Impact on Buddhist Art
key_dimensions: Pala rulers (8th–12th century CE, Bengal-Bihar): last great Buddhist imperial patrons in India
Institutions: Vikramashila, Odantapuri, Somapura Mahavihara (UNESCO site in Bangladesh)
Artistic output: Pala bronze sculpture — standardized Vajrayana iconography that influenced Nepal and Tibet
UPSC trap: Somapura Mahavihara (modern Bangladesh) was built by Dharmapala — sometimes confused with Nalanda or Vikramashila

concepts.name: Zen (Chan) Buddhism: Mahayana's East Asian Transformation
key_dimensions: Origin: blend of Mahayana Buddhism and Chinese Taoism; attributed to Bodhidharma (5th–6th century CE)
Core practice: zazen (seated meditation), koan (paradoxical riddles) for direct experience of Buddhanature
Contrast with Theravada: rejects scripture-based learning; emphasizes direct transmission 'beyond words'
UPSC trap: Zen is NOT Vajrayana despite both emphasizing direct experience — Zen is a Mahayana sub-school; Vajrayana uses Tantric rituals, Zen does not

concepts.name: Women and Monasticism Across Buddhist Schools: Bhikkhuni Sangha
key_dimensions: Buddha's reluctant establishment of the Bhikkhuni (nuns') order — Mahapajapati Gotami as first nun
Theravada: Bhikkhuni lineage died out in 11th century CE; revival controversies in Sri Lanka and Myanmar in modern times
Mahayana and Vajrayana: Bhikkhuni orders survive in China, Korea, Vietnam — full ordination available
UPSC trap: The 8 Garudhammas (special rules for nuns) placing nuns subordinate to monks — cited in debates about gender equality in Buddhism

concepts.name: B.R. Ambedkar's Neo-Buddhism (Navayana): Modern Sectarian Significance
key_dimensions: Ambedkar's 1956 conversion at Nagpur: mass conversion of Dalits — explicitly rejected caste-based Hindu social order
Navayana as a 'fourth yana': reinterprets Buddhism as a social liberation movement, rejecting rebirth/karma as explanations for caste
Selective adoption: Ambedkar accepted social ethics of Buddhism but rejected metaphysical elements (rebirth, Nirvana)
UPSC trap: Navayana is NOT recognized as a separate school by traditional Buddhist institutions (Theravada, Mahayana, Vajrayana) — it is a socio-political reinterpretation
